Feedback: I'm not an education expert, and the way I see it is but from a student's perspective. My observation does not necessarily regard underlying learning and course objectives. Having said the above, for me they would be: assessments and content. Re assessments, they're similar to traditional schools that have students memorize dates, names, etc. I guess that checks my memorization skills, but it takes away the focus I would have loved to have in actually trying to achieve the goals of a course, which are usually "to understand and be able to apply something". There are subjects that do this well (ex. EAPP-111 - the application of the modules in sentence structure), and others that I honestly find ridiculous (eg. ICT-112 - memorizing the headers of a website's column that were not mentioned in the module. I don't think we are expected to pay attention and memorize all words in a web page. It's not part of the course objective, and there's just no point to it as these are just titles to make the interface more user-friendly and have no importance in the learning outcome.) On another note, in HMRM-111, the activities had no mention of a grading system. There were questions, and I answered them based on my opinion. I don't know how my opinion was graded, or how the way I sang the hymn was checked. In general, the content, in my opinion, is really good in most subjects. There are some that are a bit overloaded (eg. ELSC-111 - videos are too long; PHIL-121 - we're supposed to read the references as well, without notice). There are those that are, I would say, quite imposing without sufficient grounds or are only based on a single/limited viewpoint (eg. "These are the best ways to do something"), or things that are not definite and still has some relativity in them such as "Chinese are better at business or at math than Filipinos". Again, I'm not an expert, but these kind of content might limit inquisitive and reasoning abilities.
